newsitem.title: USA: US Oct 1 feedlot cattle up from previous month.
newsitem.headline: US Oct 1 feedlot cattle up from previous month.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department was expected to report Friday that cattle supplies in major U.S. feedlots rose in September from the previous month, but remained below a year ago as of October 1, analysts said.

The average of analysts' estimates for the number of cattle on feed in the seven key states on October 1 was 94.8 percent of a year ago, in a range of 93 to 97 percent while September placements averaged 98.6 percent in a range of 96.0 to 104.0 percent.
The placement number is viewed as the most important number as it will influence cattle markets into next year.

"Even though it's (placements) down a little from last year, historically it's a large number so it continues the pattern of the last few months," said Tom Tippens, CEO Profesional Cattle Consultants.

USDA will release its feedlot cattle supply data at 1400 CDT/1900 GMT Friday in its Cattle-On-Feed report. This is the tenth release of the monthly 12-state report, but analysts continued to estimate data only for feedlots in the seven key states with capacities of 1,000 head or more as historical data continues to build.

September cattle placements will be compared with previous-year placements when the number of cattle put into feedlots was the highest since 1987. If September, 1996 placements were down about two percent from last year as the 98.6 percent average estimate indicates, they would be over four percent above the previous September placements in 1992 through 1995, analysts said.
Relatively large placements this year were attributed to a decline in corn prices from record highs earlier in the year.
Plenty of open pen space in feedlots following light spring placements when grain prices were soaring, also encouraged stepped-up movement of feeders into feedlots, market watchers noted.
Analysts' cattle marketing estimates for September were down from a year ago, ranging from 85 to 95 percent of last year's sales, and averaging 87.9 percent.

Some sources noted that part of the reason for the lighter marketings was a smaller number of well-finished cattle during the period. But marketings in the 80 percent area would likely still weigh on market sentiment, some sources said.
"I could see that some of the cash connected people could be disappointed with the marketing number," said Don Close, senior livestock analyst for Pioneer Hi-Bred.

Some of the feedlot people had been looking for marketings to be around 100 percent of a year ago based on the concerted effort to sell cattle and stay current. However, the rate of slaughter shows otherwise which may be viewed as bearish to markets, Close added.
